findings.title: Backup codes stored in plaintext array without hashing/removal consistency
findings.body: Backup codes are generated and encrypted as a blob, but each code remains a plaintext secret within that blob. When one code is used (next-auth-options.ts), it is replaced with null but the array length/order persists; there's no indication other than null to users which codes remain used. More importantly, codes are never hashed before storage—only the whole JSON array is symmetrically encrypted. If CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY is ever compromised, all backup codes are exposed in plaintext, unlike typical implementations where backup codes are hashed individually (similar to passwords). This is a weaker security posture than TOTP secret handling for sensitive, one-time credentials.

findings.title: backupCodes state typed as never[] causes implicit any/missing type safety
findings.body: `const [backupCodes, setBackupCodes] = useState([]);` infers backupCodes as never[], relying on implicit any assignment from setBackupCodes(body.backupCodes) where body is untyped JSON. There's no runtime validation that body.backupCodes is actually a string array, so a malformed/missing response could cause .map() to throw or silently render nothing without clear error handling.

findings.title: Setup endpoint regenerates and overwrites backup codes even if 2FA setup is abandoned
findings.body: Calling /setup regenerates backupCodes and persists them to the DB immediately (before the user confirms via /enable). If a user starts setup but never completes it (abandons at QR step), stale backup codes remain stored on the user record while twoFactorEnabled is false. These codes could later be reactivated by just calling /enable without ever being re-shown to the user, since enable.ts (not shown) presumably doesn't regenerate backup codes. This creates a risk of a backup code set associated with a now-stale/forgotten secret being usable without the owner's current knowledge of them, and multiple incomplete setup attempts quietly overwrite previous codes with no audit trail.

findings.title: Backup code match doesn't invalidate/remove the used code
findings.body: In disable.ts, after finding `index` for the supplied backup code, the comment says "we delete all stored backup codes at the end, no need to do this here" — this is true for disable flow since all backupCodes/twoFactorSecret are nulled below. However the index variable is computed but never used otherwise; this works accidentally only because disable always wipes everything. If this logic is ever reused elsewhere (e.g. refactored into a shared helper for other backup-code consuming endpoints), failing to invalidate the specific used code would allow reuse of the same backup code multiple times. There's no shared single-use enforcement abstraction, raising future reuse risk.

findings.title: No E2E coverage for backup-code login or disable-via-backup-code flow
findings.body: The PR description states backup codes can be used for login (clicking 'Lost access') and for disabling 2FA, but the only test changes added are around the backup-codes-download/copy/close UI during setup. The TODO comment explicitly acknowledges missing tests: 'add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup'. This leaves the core new login-with-backup-code and disable-with-backup-code logic (including single-use invalidation) completely untested, despite being significant new auth-critical code paths.
